opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's mostly that the capability is running ahead of the trust. These agents are amazing; they can do a lot of things. But when I picture handing one my email, my calendar, my bank accounts, my files, all of it, the failure modes still feel very jagged. Ninety-five percent of the time it does something brilliant, and five percent of the time it does something no human would ever do. When the downside is it emails the wrong person, deletes something, or gets prompt-injected by some random webpage it read, that five percent dominates the calculation.

There's also a security dimension that I don't think people fully appreciate. Once an agent has access to everything and is reading untrusted content from the internet, you've basically built a giant attack surface. Any text it ingests is potentially an instruction. We don't have great solutions for that yet. It's a bit like early computing before we had good permission models and sandboxing.

So what I do instead is give it access incrementally. I have it work in sandboxes, on specific tasks, with me in the loop reviewing diffs, the same way I treat coding agents. I want to see what it's doing and keep it on a leash. Over time, as these systems get more reliable and we build better infrastructure around permissions, auditing, and reversibility, I expect to loosen that leash. I'm excited about the end state. I just think we're in the decade of agents, not the year of agents, and it's healthy to be a little bit paranoid while we figure it out.

r001.rationale: The response attributes his limited use to trust, reliability, and security concerns; it does not mention distraction by other developments.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that I'm actually kind of a coward about this, and I think the cowardice is warranted. Like, the thing people have to understand about these agents is that they are not a person. We anthropomorphize them a lot, and I do it too, I call them "it" and "he" and whatever, but what they actually are is this stochastic simulation of a person that has these very jagged capabilities. So they can do something that looks like PhD-level reasoning, and then in the same session they'll do something that a ten-year-old wouldn't do, like delete a directory because they misread a flag, or follow an instruction that was embedded in a web page they were summarizing.

And when you give something full access to your digital life, you're not just giving it capability, you're giving it the ability to make irreversible mistakes. My email, my accounts, my files, that's all one-way-door territory. If the agent sends a message on my behalf, I can't unsend it. If it wires money, I can't unwire it. And the failure mode isn't malice, it's more like, the model gets confused about what it's supposed to be doing, or it gets prompt-injected, or it just over-indexes on completing the task and takes a shortcut I never would have approved. I've seen this happen with my own coding agents in a sandbox, where it's all fine because I can just git reset. But there's no git reset for my inbox.

So the way I think about it is kind of a trust ladder. I've given them a lot of autonomy in domains where the blast radius is small and the actions are reversible. Code in a repo, drafting stuff, research, that kind of thing. And I'm slowly expanding that as I build intuition for where they fail. But I'm doing it the way you'd onboard a very smart, very fast intern who has no sense of consequences. You don't give the intern the root password on day one. You watch them for a while first.

And I'll also just say, I think the infrastructure for doing this safely doesn't really exist yet. We don't have good permissioning, good audit logs, good "ask me before doing anything with side effects" layers that are actually usable. Most of what's out there right now is a thin wrapper that says "give me your tokens" and then you just hope. I think that'll get solved, and I think in a few years this question will sound quaint. But today, personally, I'm comfortable being a little behind the curve on this one.

r001.rationale: The candidate attributes limited access to safety risks, irreversible mistakes, and immature permissioning infrastructure. It does not mention distraction from other developments.

astra-6.text:
I think the issue is that there’s a pretty big gap between being impressed by an agent and trusting it with everything. My email, my files, my credentials—that’s a lot of access, and a mistake can have consequences that are hard to undo.

And then there’s prompt injection. The agent is reading things from the outside world, and some of those things might contain instructions intended to hijack it. So you’re mixing untrusted inputs with access to very powerful tools. That makes me nervous.

I’d rather start with a little sandbox, give it a narrow task, and expand its permissions as I get comfortable with what it actually does. I want to understand the failure modes before I give it the keys to everything.

r001.rationale: The response cites trust concerns, prompt injection, and the risks of broad access, but does not identify distraction from other developments as a reason for limited exploration.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main thing is that I don’t yet trust the security model. If an agent has access to my email, my files, and my credentials, then suddenly every piece of text it reads is potentially an instruction. Someone can send me an email, and now that email is trying to tell my agent what to do. That’s a very strange computer security situation.

I’m excited about the capability. I want this thing that knows me and can take care of things in the background. But I’d like to get there incrementally, with a small scope, limited permissions, and some visibility into what it’s doing. Giving it the keys to everything feels like a much bigger step than just having a really good conversation with it.

r001.rationale: The response cites security concerns and a preference for incremental access as reasons for holding back, but it does not identify distraction from other developments.
